Senate Majority Leader John Thune said in a brief interview Thursday that he is currently staying out of the dispute. “I haven't weighed into that,” he said, adding that he told Murkowski that she and Moran “need to talk it out” and that “we’ll see where those conversations lead."

But Moran said the two have already discussed the issue, and neither is budging. “She and I have been talking on several occasions since this began,” he said. “But I'm not sure how you talk this to a conclusion.”

Moran said GOP senators on the Appropriations Committee will first weigh in, followed by a vote by all Senate Republicans. While it’s possible internal conference decisions could be made this year, the Senate is set to ratify those selections on the floor in early January.

Moran would not say whether he would stop pursuing his party's top committee spot if he were promised a choice subcommittee perch like leading the defense funding panel. But he said Murkowski intends to take the top Republican spot on both the full committee and the coveted subcommittee in charge of doling out roughly $1 trillion for military programs each year.

Asked about Moran’s challenge, Murkowski said Thursday that she would “rather talk with members than talk through the press,” adding, “I think that's how we respect one another.”

item.title: Trump renews calls for $350B military funding package as GOP faces ticking clock
item.description: Prior demands for party-line Pentagon spending have stalled on Capitol Hill. Now Democratic control is imminent.

media:content.media:title: Senate Republican Leader John Thune looks downward as reporters ask him questions on Capitol Hill on Nov. 9, 2026.

item.dc:creator: By Mia McCarthy and Jordain Carney
item.dc:contributor: By Mia McCarthy and Jordain Carney
item.content:encoded:
President Donald Trump called on Senate Republicans Thursday to use their final weeks in power to pass $350 billion in defense spending — moving to jump-start legislative action “IMMEDIATELY” on a party-line funding request that has gone unanswered for months.

“Our Military must be strong, powerful, and respected,” Trump said in a Truth Social post. “Republicans must deliver for our Warriors. The Democrats never will. The time is NOW.”

The post comes as Republicans face scant time on Capitol Hill to make progress on key priorities before Democrats assume the big new majorities they won in last week’s midterms. Democratic leaders in both parties are signaling they will seek to end the Iran war — possibly by blocking funding as soon as next month.

But Trump’s previous calls to enact massive new infusions of Pentagon funding have gone unheeded in the Senate, where GOP lawmakers have split over how to structure a party-line spending bill.

A House-passed budget blueprint that includes Iran war funding has stalled in the Senate for nearly four months but even that legislation provides only $60 billion for the Pentagon — a fraction of the funding Trump is asking for.

Senate Majority Leader John Thune said this week he remained “open” to pursuing a party-line funding bill under the budget reconciliation process but also said he believed the House needed to act first.

“We’ll see if there’s a political appetite to do it,” he told reporters Monday. “It takes a lot of time, as you know, and … to get all this other stuff done.”

Thune and Rep. Jim Jordan (R-Ohio), the incoming House minority leader, discussed the prospects for reconciliation during a closed-door meeting Wednesday, the first time they had met in person since winning their respective leadership elections.

Senate Republicans discussed trying to pass a new reconciliation bill during an hourslong meeting ahead of their leadership election Tuesday and effectively agreed to try to see if they could find a path, several senators said after the meeting.

But some GOP senators, including party leaders, have been skeptical that there are the votes to pass another party-line spending bill amid divisions over what should be included in it.

Sen. John Kennedy (R-La.), a member of the Senate Budget Committee, said Republicans’ best shot would be to keep any bill narrowly focused on only a couple of items.

“I think we ought to actually try to get a result, and the worst we can do is lose,” Kennedy said in an interview. “I don’t think, to be fair, that leadership agrees with me.”

Senate Budget Chair Ron Johnson (R-Wis.) said Thursday that he believed it was “good” that the president was engaged and that the request matches what he’s heard privately from top Pentagon officials. But he would not say if Republicans have the votes.

Thune said this week Republicans would have to make a decision by Thanksgiving and noted the lengthy process required to enact a reconciliation bill. Johnson said he wants a budget blueprint on the Senate floor before lawmakers leave for the upcoming holiday next week.

Prior to Trump’s posting Thursday, House Majority Leader Steve Scalise said in an interview that he wanted to see a “broad reconciliation bill move in the lame duck.”

“We started that process. We passed it through the House. Hopefully, now that the elections are over, the Senate gets back to it,” Scalise said Thursday.

Also speaking before Trump leveled his demand, Speaker Mike Johnson pointed fingers at Senate Democrats Thursday for having “obstructed everything” — though it is GOP divisions that have left the chamber sitting on the House-passed budget blueprint, a key prerequisite for the party-line reconciliation process.

“This is a two-chamber legislative body, so we need the Senate to do their work,” Johnson said.

Katherine Tully-McManus contributed to this report.

item.title: Senate committee schedules nomination hearing for top Trump watchdog as Democrats cry ‘sham’
item.description: Democrats are accusing GOP congressional leaders of helping the president install one of his allies atop the Government Accountability Office.

media:content.media:title: Senate Homeland Security Chair Rand Paul (R-Ky.) gavels in a meeting to consider a resolution to hold Anthony Fauci in contempt of Congress on Capitol Hill on Aug. 6, 2026.

item.dc:creator: By Jennifer Scholtes
item.content:encoded:
The Senate is scheduled to hold a hearing next week on President Donald Trump still-secret nominee to run the Government Accountability Office as Democrats accuse Republicans of colluding to install a Trump ally.

The Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee is slated to hear testimony from a slew of Trump nominees Thursday morning, including “a nominee to be comptroller general.” The president has yet to nominate anyone to that post, however, and a bipartisan panel of 10 lawmakers is supposed to first recommend a list of candidates to the White House for consideration.

Top Democrats divulged Wednesday night that they were given less than 24 hours to submit suggestions, accusing Republicans of running a "sham" process to help Trump put “a fox in the henhouse” at the agency charged with aiding and protecting Congress’ authority to push back against overstep by the executive branch.

The role of comptroller general has taken on new significance during Trump’s second term, as the president continues to shirk Congress’ funding directive after the Supreme Court suggested last year that the watchdog may be the only entity with standing to sue the Trump administration under decades-old impoundment law.

item.title: China panel chair still wants Huang to testify after Nvidia exit
item.description: Rep. John Moolenaar said he would look to subpoena the executive if they cannot agree on a date.

media:content.media:title: Chair John Moolenaar speaks during a House Select Committee on the Chinese Communist Party hearing on July 23, 2025, in Washington.

item.dc:creator: By Owen Dahlkamp and Kelsey Brugger
item.dc:contributor: By Owen Dahlkamp and Kelsey Brugger
item.content:encoded:
House China Select Committee Chair John Moolenaar (R-Mich.) said he wants to call Jensen Huang before Congress, despite the former CEO resigning from Nvidia on Thursday.

“We are in discussions with him right now on a date to come and meet with us,” he told reporters.

Moolenaar said he, House Intelligence Chair Rick Crawford (R-Ark.) and House Foreign Affairs Chair Brian Mast (R-Fla.) are prepared to subpoena Huang if they cannot agree on a date.

The trio sent a letter to Huang last week summoning him to Capitol Hill. Moolenaar said they received a response yesterday but declined to provide further detail.

Nvidia’s board on Thursday morning announced that Huang had stepped down as CEO, president and board chair. Current Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress has taken over as interim CEO.

Moolenaar said he’d like to use the hearing to understand how Chinese intelligence operated, what information was accessed and how Huang has lobbied for policy changes on behalf of the company, including over the export of its cutting-edge chips.

New York Rep. Gregory Meeks, the top Democrat on the House Foreign Affairs Committee, said Thursday he hasn’t spoken to his Republican counterpart yet but that he’s preparing to create a subcommittee next Congress to focus on the questions surrounding the fallout of Huang’s affairs.

“We may very well be setting up a subcommittee just focused on some of this stuff because that's how important and significant it is,” he said, adding he wanted to approach the issue in a bipartisan way.

“I can guarantee you,” he told reporters. “Come Jan. 4, there will be some hearings.”

Nvidia did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

item.title: Capitol agenda: Freedom Caucus navigates a Jordan-led GOP
item.description: Jordan’s ascendance is prompting big questions about the role of a group that was established to prod party leaders rightward now that the GOP’s top man is one of their own.

media:content.media:title: Rep. Clay Higgins speaks alongside Reps. Ralph Norman, Andy Harris, Randy Fine, Keith Self and Mary Miller during a House Freedom Caucus press conference on Capitol Hill on Nov. 11, 2026.

item.dc:creator: By Calen Razor
item.content:encoded:
Jim Jordan was elected as the top House Republican. Now the relevance of the hard-line Freedom Caucus is in question.

Jordan is one of the ultra-conservative group’s co-founders and its very first chair back in 2015. The splinter faction since then has wielded its power by acting as a holdout bloc in GOP majorities, with former Speaker John Boehner once labeling Jordan a “legislative terrorist.”

But now Jordan is poised to helm a GOP on track to hold the smallest House minority any party has had in more than 30 years, with many influential Freedom Caucus veterans also leaving the House after this term.

Jordan’s ascendance is prompting big questions about the role of a group that was established to prod party leaders rightward now that the GOP’s top man is one of their own.

“It’s completely variant from being the most powerful faction within a legislative body that has legislative authority through majority control,” said Rep. Clay Higgins, a caucus member. “Well, that’s off the table now.”

At a Wednesday news conference, several members rejected the notion that there would be any diminishment of its influence. But many also believe Jordan in leadership will change how the group functions.

Higgins insisted the group’s “principles are the same” but it’ll be more focused on “strategic alignment to protect the gains that we have indeed made over the last few years.”

Others acknowledged in some fashion that the group’s relationship with Jordan — who is still a member, according to a spokesperson — could be complicated.

“It’s like when you hire your brother to build your house,” Rep. Eric Burlison, who is running this month for caucus chair, said in an interview. “There may be some awkward moments, but at the end of the day, we have a shared goal and a shared vision.”

While current Freedom Caucus members see his promotion as a win overall, they also said they understand he now has a mandate to lead the full range of GOP members.

“The further you go up in leadership, the broader your responsibility,” said Rep. Keith Self. “So we don’t expect him to be a direct advocate for HFC. He will certainly be a friend of HFC.”

What else we’re watching: 

— GOP TURNS ON LUTNICK OVER NVIDIA: Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick and other agency leaders are in Hill Republican’s crosshairs as the impact of Nvidia’s espionage scandal unfolds. Recent reports that the Commerce Department failed to take action on the firm at the center of the spying and chip-smuggling allegations have intensified scrutiny of the agency’s decisions to allow more foreign chip sales, particularly from Nvidia. Over the past 24 hours, more than half a dozen Republicans have demanded answers from Lutnick and top deputies over whether they put private tech interests above national security.
 
— HIMES URGES GOP TO TAKE FISA ‘WIN’ — House Intelligence Committee ranking member Jim Himes is urging Senate leadership to reauthorize a key spy program during the lame-duck session rather than waiting for the new Congress. Himes, who is likely to take over the House Intelligence panel next year, told POLITICO that he recently spoke with Senate Majority Leader John Thune about reauthorizing Section 702 of the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act. The program is due to expire in March, but intelligence officials have warned that there may be a lag in the needed judicial go-ahead if it isn’t renewed by the end of this month.
 
Mia McCarthy, Ari Hawkins, Gabby Miller, Jordain Carney, Katherine Hapgood, Maggie Miller and Gregory Svirnovskiy contributed to this report.

item.title: The Freedom Caucus comes to grips with a new reality: They won the war
item.description: The group’s co-founder is now the top House Republican leader, posing an identity crisis for the hard-line splinter faction.

media:content.media:title: Rep. Andy Harris (R-Md.), outgoing chair of the House Freedom Caucus, speaks alongside other members of the Freedom Caucus during a press conference on Capitol Hill in Washington, on Nov. 11, 2026.

item.dc:creator: By Mia McCarthy
item.content:encoded:
The House Freedom Caucus is staring down an unfamiliar new reality in 2027: questionable relevance.

That’s partly because the ultra-conservative group achieved an indubitable triumph this week, when its co-founder and first chair, Ohio Rep. Jim Jordan, was elected Tuesday to serve as the next top House Republican leader.

It’s also because the group has traditionally wielded its power by acting as a holdout bloc in thin Republican majorities. Now the GOP is on track to hold the smallest House minority any party has had in more than 30 years.

“It's completely variant from being the most powerful faction within a legislative body that has legislative authority through majority control,” said Rep. Clay Higgins of Louisiana, a caucus member. “Well, that's off the table now.”

Founded in 2015, the Freedom Caucus persisted through a prior stretch in the minority, under then-Leader Kevin McCarthy, from 2019 to 2023. But Jordan’s ascendance is prompting big questions about the role of a group that was established to prod party leaders rightward now that the GOP’s top man is one of their own.

Higgins said, for example, “our principles are the same” but the group would now be more focused on “strategic alignment to protect the gains that we have indeed made over the last few years.” Another member, Rep. Marlin Stutzman of Indiana, said it would move to a “think tank model where we're pulling good information together … to really inform the rest of the conference.”

At a Wednesday news conference where members of the group blamed the GOP’s huge election losses on current party leaders’ timidity, several rejected the notion that there would be any diminishment of its influence — including several who are expected to vie to be elected caucus chair in the next Congress.

Asked what the point of the Freedom Caucus was with Jordan as leader, Rep. Andrew Clyde of Georgia scoffed: “What you're saying, basically, is that the whole entity of the Freedom Caucus can be found in one man. That's not right.”

But others acknowledged in some fashion that the group’s relationship with Jordan could be complicated.

Rep. Eric Burlison of Missouri, who like Clyde is running for caucus chair, said he expected that the group would have to pressure Jordan at times.

“It's like when you hire your brother to build your house,” Burlison said in an interview. “There may be some awkward moments, but at the end of the day, we have a shared goal and a shared vision.”

How the Freedom Caucus can deliver pressure is in doubt. In the past it has asserted itself on procedural votes and other matters where it has enough numbers to deny GOP leaders a Republican majority on the floor. That logic simply does not hold in the minority, where it’s generally easier for the out-party to unite against the majority.

Members of the group have joked, “When you’re in the minority, everyone’s in the Freedom Caucus.”

The group is also suffering from the loss of several influential veteran members, such as Reps. Chip Roy of Texas, Ralph Norman of South Carolina and Andy Biggs of Arizona — who all lost bids for higher office. Reps. Scott Perry of Pennsylvania, a former chair like Biggs, lost his seat to a Democrat, and Rep. Lauren Boebert of Colorado is trailing in her race.

The Freedom Caucus’ political arm also failed to make serious gains during the midterms, spending in several races but only winning a handful after a particularly brutal primary season.

Several potential GOP newcomers have shown interest in joining the group, according to Rep. Andy Harris of Maryland, the outgoing chair. He predicted that the Freedom Caucus would have more members by the midpoint of the upcoming Congress than it has in the current one.

While current members see Jordan’s promotion as a huge win for the group, they also said they understand he now has a mandate to lead the full range of GOP members.

That’s how Jordan has acted more recently, anyway. He attempted to make inroads with GOP moderates ahead of his leader run and otherwise adopted a more mellow approach from the days more than a decade ago when then-Speaker John Boehner referred to him as a “legislative terrorist.”

Jordan has been a less central presence in the Freedom Caucus in recent years but still frequently attends its meetings. A spokesperson said Jordan still considers himself a member of the Freedom Caucus as well as the Republican Study Committee, a larger and less militant conservative group.

When asked after his election Tuesday about his role, Jordan said it is to “help House Republicans get back to the majority.” The spokesperson responded to a question about his future relationship with the Freedom Caucus by saying, “We look forward to working with the entire Republican conference to unite against and defeat the radical Democrat agenda.”

“The further you go up in leadership, the broader your responsibility,” Rep. Keith Self of Texas said. “So we don't expect him to be a direct advocate for HFC. He will certainly be a friend of HFC.”

Those outside the group are puzzling out how they’ll adapt to the new reality. Rep. Chris Smith of New Jersey, one of the two longest-serving House Republicans, said it will “have relevance, but I'm not sure what their issues will be.”

Smith added Jordan is “going to be very faithful to what the conference wants him to do.”

Asked if Jordan might need to be pushed right on occasion, Harris said there’s “no question” that he is a conservative and praised him as “a superb communicator” and “exactly what we need.”

Several members predicted the Freedom Caucus could serve as an internal heat shield for Jordan — giving him cover to build support for more conservative positions as he works with President Donald Trump to battle Democrats.

“Jim will still need the deep rudder of this ship to guide the Republican Conference,” Higgins said. “He'll need us to align strategically and be willing to draw lines in the sand that would be more difficult for him to do as the leader of the conference.”

item.title: Democrats accuse GOP of helping Trump put ‘fox in the henhouse’ at top watchdog
item.description: They warn that Republicans are driving a “sham” process to pick the next Government Accountability Office head.

media:content.media:title: Sen. Rand Paul (R-Ky.) speaks during a Senate Foreign Relations Committee hearing on Capitol Hill Jan. 28, 2026.

item.dc:creator: By Jennifer Scholtes
item.content:encoded:
Congressional Democrats claim GOP leaders are trying to choke off the selection process for the federal government’s top watchdog in a bid to let President Donald Trump install one of his allies before Republicans cede the majority in January.

Top Democrats in both chambers divulged Wednesday night that Republicans gave them less than 24 hours to submit candidates to serve as Comptroller General, otherwise known as the head of the Government Accountability Office — an official uniquely empowered to sue Trump on Congress’ behalf for clawing back federal funding lawmakers have approved.

“This is clearly a sham to enable President Trump to appoint a handpicked nominee to lead Congress’ watchdog,” the Democrats said in a joint statement. “We cannot allow President Trump to install a fox in the henhouse at an agency Congress relies on to provide independent, nonpartisan oversight, and expose waste, fraud, and abuse across the Trump Administration.”

The lawmakers signing onto the statement include Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer and House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, and the top Democrats on the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee and the Committee on House Oversight and Governmental Affairs — Gary Peters of Michigan and Robert Garcia of California, respectively.

GAO is currently headed by an acting comptroller general, Orice Williams Brown, who is under increasing pressure to sue the Trump administration for withholding federal cash after the president canceled hundreds of millions of dollars without Congress’ consent this fall. Brown assumed that role last December, when Gene Dodaro retired at the end of his 15-year term.

By law, a bipartisan panel of 10 lawmakers is supposed to recommend candidates for Trump to nominate for Senate confirmation. And when Dodaro retired last year, Senate HSGAC Chair Rand Paul (R-Ky.) — one of the lawmakers on the broader recommendation committee — said he intended to “look for someone who’s honest,” warning that it would be “a mistake to get somebody who’s been real active in political processes.”

Democrats now claim Paul and other top Republicans are working to “ram through another Trump crony at the 11th hour, and undercut Congress’ ability to conduct effective oversight of the Trump Administration.”

The Washington Sun reported last month that the administration has floated the idea of nominating Eric Ueland to head GAO; POLITICO has not independently confirmed that the White House is considering the former longtime Senate aide who now serves as a senior official at the White House budget office.

In the months leading up to Dodaro’s retirement last year, Democrats on Capitol Hill began to lament the fact that a president who continually challenges the bounds of Congress’ funding power would get to nominate the watchdog tasked with defending the authority of the legislative branch.

In the more than 10 months since Dodaro left the role, Republican leaders on the bipartisan selection commission have held no meetings, nor have they interviewed any candidates for the role, said Schumer, Jeffries, Peters and Garcia Wednesday night.

Peters and Garcia are supposed to be on the panel that recommends GAO candidates, since they are the leading Democrats on Congress’ oversight committees.

Spokespeople for Paul and Senate Majority Leader John Thune did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

item.title: Brian Poindexter disappears from Democratic groups’ endorsement lists
item.description: The Ohioan defeated Republican Rep. Max Miller in a closely watched race.

media:content.media:title: Rep.-elect Brian Poindexter (D-Ohio) arrives at the AC Hotel during new member orientation in Washington on Nov. 8, 2026.

item.dc:creator: By Riley Rogerson
item.content:encoded:
The political arms of two influential Democratic caucuses removed Ohio candidate Brian Poindexter from their endorsement list in the days around his closely watched House election win.

Blue Dog PAC, the campaign wing of the moderate Blue Dog Coalition, listed Poindexter among their endorsees as of Oct. 28, and Congressional Progressive Caucus PAC listed him as of Nov. 1, according to webpages cached by the Internet Archive.

It was an unusual feat to earn backing from the two groups, who are seen as representing opposite poles of the House Democratic Caucus. But now neither group lists Poindexter, who defeated embattled GOP Rep. Max Miller in a Cleveland-area district, among their endorsees.

The removals are especially notable given Poindexter’s victory in a high-profile race that garnered headlines due to allegations of domestic abuse against Miller, which he has denied.

Members and aides connected to the two groups did not offer answers about what happened. Spokespeople for Blue Dog PAC and CPC PAC did not return requests for comment.

Two Progressive Caucus leaders, Reps. Pramila Jayapal of Washington and Greg Casar of Texas, declined to comment when asked about the endorsements Wednesday on Capitol Hill.

Rep. Jared Golden of Maine, a senior Blue Dogs member, spoke only briefly Wednesday: “I don't have much to say about it. We decided that it’s not a good fit.”

When asked about the endorsements during a brief interview on Capitol Hill, Poindexter said Tuesday, “My main focus right now is just setting up my office and stuff. There could be time to join ideological caucuses.”

Poindexter did not deny that his name was removed: “I just said I wanted to hold off before I join up a caucus. I wanted to hold off a little while.”

He added, “Nothing to read into that. Just, I’m waiting to learn the political landscape.”

Chris Marquette contributed to this report.
